note: Curated, human-reviewed facts. Every entry names the source it was checked against; the build refuses any entry with `verified: false` or an empty `source_detail`.

facts.headline: Basketball invented the shot clock because one game finished 19–18.
facts.body: On 22 November 1950 the Fort Wayne Pistons held the ball for minutes at a time and beat the Minneapolis Lakers 19–18, still the lowest-scoring game in league history. Four years later the NBA adopted a 24-second clock, and scoring jumped 13.6 points a game in a single season.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: NBA.com and Naismith Basketball Hall of Fame accounts of the 24-second clock's adoption; Time, 'How the Shot Clock Saved Basketball'

facts.headline: The 24-second clock is not a round number. It is division.
facts.body: Danny Biasone, who owned the Syracuse Nationals, took the 2,880 seconds in a game and divided by the 120 shots two teams were then averaging between them. The answer was 24, and it is still the number the professional game runs on.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: NBA.com and Naismith Basketball Hall of Fame accounts of the 24-second clock's adoption; Time, 'How the Shot Clock Saved Basketball'

facts.headline: Nobody filmed the 100-point game.
facts.body: Wilt Chamberlain scored 100 in Hershey, Pennsylvania on 2 March 1962 as Philadelphia beat New York 169–147. No television cameras were there. What survives is a fourth-quarter radio recording made by a college student on a rigged aerial — now held by the Library of Congress.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: Library of Congress National Recording Preservation Board, 'Fourth quarter radio coverage of Wilt Chamberlain's 100-point game'; NBA.com top moments, 1962

facts.headline: The Dream Team exists because of a vote the United States lost.
facts.body: In Munich in April 1989, FIBA voted 56–13 to let professionals into the Olympics. USA Basketball voted against it. Three years later the Dream Team walked into Barcelona.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: Olympics.com and Britannica accounts of FIBA's April 1989 Munich vote and the 1992 Barcelona tournament

facts.headline: The Dream Team's first Olympic opponent was Angola.
facts.body: On 26 July 1992 the first team of NBA professionals ever to play at an Olympics beat Angola 116–48. The 68-point margin remains the tournament's most quoted number, and Angola's players asked for photographs afterwards.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: Olympics.com and Britannica accounts of FIBA's April 1989 Munich vote and the 1992 Barcelona tournament

facts.headline: The first three-pointer in NBA history was a formality nobody wanted.
facts.body: The league adopted the line for 1979–80 as a one-year trial, three years after inheriting it from the ABA and declining to use it. Chris Ford of the Celtics made the first one on 12 October 1979 against Houston.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: NBA.com, 'Doubt, disdain marked most NBA teams' first forays into 3-point land'; CBS Sports on the 1994-97 shortened line

facts.headline: For three seasons the NBA moved the three-point line in, and it backfired.
facts.body: From 1994–95 the arc was a uniform 22 feet, 21 inches closer at the top. Attempts rose by more than half — and scoring kept falling. The line went back where it was after 1996–97 and has not moved since.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: NBA.com, 'Doubt, disdain marked most NBA teams' first forays into 3-point land'; CBS Sports on the 1994-97 shortened line

facts.headline: Kareem Abdul-Jabbar's first NBA game was a 29-point double-double.
facts.body: 18 October 1969, for Milwaukee against Detroit: 29 points and 12 rebounds, at 22 years old. He would go on to hold the league's career scoring record for 39 years.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: NBA.com 'This Week in History: Kareem Abdul-Jabbar's NBA Debut'; Basketball-Reference game log, 18 October 1969

facts.headline: One record stood for 39 years and fell on a turnaround jumper.
facts.body: On 7 February 2023, with 10.9 seconds left in the third quarter, LeBron James hit a 21-footer for his 38,388th point and passed Kareem Abdul-Jabbar. Abdul-Jabbar had held the record since 1984.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: NBA.com scoring tracker and NPR/CNN reports of 7 February 2023

facts.headline: The only Latin American team ever to win Olympic basketball gold did it by beating the United States.
facts.body: Argentina knocked the Americans out 89–81 in the 2004 semi-final, Manu Ginóbili scoring 29, then beat Italy for gold. Since men's basketball entered the Games in 1936, no other side from the region has won it.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: Olympics.com, 'We broke the spell, the aura of the invincible USA'; ESPN on Argentina's 2004 gold

facts.headline: The WNBA's first game was played in a building the Lakers had just left.
facts.body: The New York Liberty and Los Angeles Sparks opened the league on 21 June 1997 at the Great Western Forum. Eight teams started: Charlotte, Cleveland, Houston, Los Angeles, New York, Phoenix, Sacramento and Utah.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: WNBA.com history timeline; ESPN, 'Inside the WNBA's inaugural game, 25 seasons later'

facts.headline: The WNBA's first signed player was pregnant for its first season.
facts.body: Sheryl Swoopes was announced on 23 October 1996, before the league had played a game. She gave birth six weeks into the inaugural season, returned that summer, and won the first four championships with Houston.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: WNBA.com history timeline; ESPN, 'Inside the WNBA's inaugural game, 25 seasons later'

facts.headline: Diana Taurasi finished her career more than 2,500 points clear of everyone.
facts.body: Twenty WNBA seasons, three championships, six Olympic golds, and the league's career records for points, field goals and three-pointers. The scoring margin over second place is larger than many careers.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: ESPN and WNBA.com on Diana Taurasi's career scoring record and 2025 retirement

facts.headline: The WNBA's 2024 attendance jump was the largest in its history.
facts.body: The league averaged 9,807 a game, up from 6,615 the year before, and a Fever–Mystics game drew 20,711 to Capital One Arena — the biggest regular-season crowd the league had ever had.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: Sportico and Bleacher Report on 2024 WNBA attendance; ESPN on the league's season totals

facts.headline: Basketball was invented in two weeks, with a soccer ball and two peach baskets.
facts.body: James Naismith, a Canadian teaching in Springfield, Massachusetts, was given a fortnight to devise an indoor winter game. He wrote thirteen rules and nailed the baskets to the gymnasium balcony — which is why the rim is ten feet up.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: Springfield College, 'Where Basketball was Invented'; Smithsonian Magazine and National Geographic accounts of 1891

facts.headline: Europe's most successful basketball club has more continental titles than any NBA franchise has championships.
facts.body: Real Madrid has won eleven European crowns. Panathinaikos, second on the list, won a seventh in 2024 after a thirteen-year wait, beating Real Madrid in the Final Four along the way.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: Olympics.com and Euronews on the 2024 EuroLeague Final Four and all-time EuroLeague titles

facts.headline: Australia's national league is older than the three-point line's permanence in the NBA.
facts.body: The NBL was founded in 1979 — the same season the NBA first tried the three-pointer — and now runs with ten teams, nine Australian and one from New Zealand.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: NBL Australia official site and league records

facts.headline: Yao Ming ran Chinese basketball for longer than he played in the NBA.
facts.body: Nine seasons in Houston, all of them; before that, the Shanghai Sharks. He was elected chairman of the Chinese Basketball Association in February 2017 and held the role for years afterwards.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: Britannica biography of Yao Ming; ESPN and NBA.com on his CBA chairmanship

facts.headline: The most second-guessed pick in NBA history was made by a team that already had a shooting guard.
facts.body: Portland took Sam Bowie second in 1984 and Michael Jordan went third to Chicago. Bowie was a seven-foot centre; the Blazers had drafted Clyde Drexler the year before.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: Britannica, 'Who was drafted ahead of Michael Jordan?'; 1984 NBA draft records

facts.headline: Only one player from the 1999 NBA draft is in the Hall of Fame, and he was picked 57th.
facts.body: San Antonio took Manu Ginóbili with the second-to-last pick of the second round. He did not arrive in the NBA for another three years.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: Basketball-Reference draft record, 1999; Pounding The Rock on the 1999 class's only Hall of Famer

facts.headline: Nikola Jokić was drafted 41st, and the pick was announced during a commercial break.
facts.body: Denver took him in the second round in 2014, forty places after the first centre off the board. He had never played outside Serbia.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: NBA Draft and Denver Nuggets records, 2014 second round; ESPN, 'Why was Finals MVP Nikola Jokic the 41st pick?'

facts.headline: The longest winning streak in major American professional sport is 33 games, and it is more than fifty years old.
facts.body: The 1971–72 Lakers won every game from 5 November to 9 January. The team that finally beat them was Milwaukee, with Kareem Abdul-Jabbar and Oscar Robertson.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: NBA.com Lakers, 'The '72 Lakers' 33-Game Win Streak'; NBA.com on the Bucks ending it

facts.headline: The man who ended the Lakers' 33-game streak spent the second half of his career winning titles for them.
facts.body: Kareem Abdul-Jabbar's Bucks stopped the run on 9 January 1972. He was traded to Los Angeles in 1975 and won five championships in the same uniform he had beaten.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: NBA.com Lakers, 'The '72 Lakers' 33-Game Win Streak'; NBA.com on the Bucks ending it — cross-referenced with Abdul-Jabbar's career record on Basketball-Reference

facts.headline: Willis Reed scored four points in the most famous game of his life.
facts.body: He tore a thigh muscle in Game 5 of the 1970 Finals, missed Game 6, and walked out of the tunnel for Game 7. He made the Knicks' first two baskets and almost nothing after that. New York won 113–99.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: NBA.com top Finals moments, 1970 Game 7; Naismith Hall of Fame biography of Willis Reed

facts.headline: The Flu Game was Game 5, not Game 6, and it was not the closer.
facts.body: Michael Jordan scored 38 against Utah on 11 June 1997 while barely able to stand, and hit a three in the last half-minute for the lead. The series still needed another game.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: NBA.com top Finals moments, 'Michael Jordan flu game', 1997 Game 5

facts.headline: The most famous shot of the 2013 Finals only happened because of an offensive rebound.
facts.body: Miami were three down with the clock off. LeBron James missed; Chris Bosh out-jumped two Spurs for the ball; Ray Allen backpedalled into the right corner and tied it with 5.2 seconds left. Miami won that game in overtime and the series in seven.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: NBA.com top Finals moments, 'Ray Allen 3-pointer, Game 6, 2013 Finals'

facts.headline: Robert Horry has more championship rings than Michael Jordan, and was never an All-Star.
facts.body: Seven, with three different franchises: two in Houston, three in Los Angeles, two in San Antonio. He averaged seven points a game for his career.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: Basketball-Reference career record; San Antonio Sports Hall of Fame biography

facts.headline: One franchise won eight championships in a row. No other has won four.
facts.body: Boston took every title from 1959 to 1966 under Red Auerbach, with Bill Russell at centre for all of them — eleven in thirteen seasons. The longest run by anybody else is three.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: NBA.com, 'Boston Celtics' NBA championships'; Britannica on the 1959-66 run

facts.headline: One rule change added more scoring in a season than the three-point line ever has.
facts.body: NBA teams averaged 79.5 points a game in 1953–54. With the 24-second clock, they averaged 93.1 the following season — a 13.6-point jump from a single rule.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: NBA.com and Naismith Basketball Hall of Fame accounts of the 24-second clock's adoption; Time, 'How the Shot Clock Saved Basketball'

facts.headline: The NBA spent three years with the three-point line in its possession and refused to use it.
facts.body: The ABA had used the shot since 1967. The leagues merged in 1976, four ABA teams joined, and the line stayed off NBA floors until 1979–80 — adopted then only as a one-year experiment.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: NBA.com, 'Doubt, disdain marked most NBA teams' first forays into 3-point land'; CBS Sports on the 1994-97 shortened line

facts.headline: The first Olympic basketball final was played outdoors, in the rain, and finished 19–8.
facts.body: Berlin, 1936, on converted tennis courts. The United States beat Canada in conditions that made dribbling close to impossible. No Olympic basketball game has been played outdoors since.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: FIBA, 'Olympic Games: Berlin 1936'; Olympics.com, 'Olympic basketball's muddy beginnings'

facts.headline: The last three seconds of the 1972 Olympic final were played three times.
facts.body: Confusion over a timeout and the game clock sent Munich back to the same three seconds twice more. The Soviet Union won 51–50, ending a 64-game American Olympic winning streak, and the United States has never accepted the silver medals.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: Wikipedia and HISTORY accounts of the 1972 Olympic men's basketball final; 'Three Seconds in Munich' (University of Nebraska Press)

facts.headline: Lithuania went to the 1992 Olympics in tie-dye paid for by the Grateful Dead.
facts.body: Newly independent and short of money, the team was funded by the band, who also sent the uniforms: tie-dye, with a slam-dunking skeleton on the front. Lithuania won bronze wearing them.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: Snopes fact-check, 'Did the Grateful Dead Fund Lithuania's Olympic Basketball Team?'; Ultimate Classic Rock and Sports History Weekly accounts

facts.headline: Lithuania calls basketball its second religion, and means it almost literally.
facts.body: The saying places it behind Catholicism and nothing else. A country of under three million has produced Olympic medals, EuroLeague champions and a steady line of NBA players.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: Lithuania Travel, 'The Second Religion of Lithuania'; Global Times, 'In Lithuania, basketball is second only to God'

facts.headline: Portland drafted Arvydas Sabonis in 1986 and did not see him play until 1995.
facts.body: He was 24th overall, behind the Iron Curtain, and by the time he arrived his knees had taken the best of him. He still made an All-Rookie team at 31.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: Wikipedia and Blazer's Edge accounts of the 1986 NBA draft and Arvydas Sabonis's arrival in Portland

facts.headline: Dražen Petrović was a second-round pick who changed how the NBA saw European guards.
facts.body: Portland took him in 1986 and he arrived in 1989. By his fourth season in New Jersey he was playing at an All-Star level; he was killed in a car accident in 1993, aged 28.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: ESPN, 'Drazen Petrovic leaves lasting legacy in NBA'; 1986 NBA draft records

facts.headline: The most prolific scorer in basketball history never played a minute in the NBA.
facts.body: Oscar Schmidt turned down New Jersey after the 1984 draft because signing would have meant leaving Brazil's national team. He finished with 49,737 points for club and country — a total LeBron James did not pass until 2024.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: NBA.com and Olympics.com obituaries of Oscar Schmidt; Naismith Hall of Fame biography

facts.headline: The NBA's African league tipped off in Kigali, in front of a continent that had waited decades for one.
facts.body: The Basketball Africa League played its first season in Rwanda in May 2021, with twelve champion clubs from across the continent. It is the first league the NBA has helped run outside North America.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: NBA Africa press release, 'Basketball Africa League 2021: By the Numbers'; Atlantic Council, 'The Basketball Africa League has arrived'

facts.headline: In the Philippines the basketball court is a piece of civic infrastructure.
facts.body: Barangays — the country's smallest administrative unit — build and maintain them the way other places build playgrounds, and a single neighbourhood can hold several. It is the most popular sport in the country by a distance.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: Asia Society, '15 Photos Exploring the Filipino Obsession With Basketball'; National Geographic's 'Pinoy Hoops'

facts.headline: The NBA got rid of one defensive habit and scoring went up by three and a half points a game.
facts.body: Hand-checking — a defender resting a hand on the ball-handler to steer him — was outlawed for 2004-05. Teams averaged 93.7 points the season before and 97.2 the season after.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: Sportskeeda and Basketball Network accounts of the 2004-05 hand-checking change and the scoring shift that followed

facts.headline: The NBA banned zone defence for decades, then legalised it and added a rule to stop it working.
facts.body: Zones became legal for 2001-02, and the defensive three-second violation arrived in the same package — a defender may not camp in the paint. One change opened the door; the other kept anyone from standing in it.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: Wikipedia, 'Defensive three-second violation'; NBA rule-change records for 2001-02

facts.headline: The draft lottery exists because teams were visibly trying to lose.
facts.body: Before 1985 the worst record got the first pick, and the incentive was exactly what it looks like. The first lottery sent Patrick Ewing to New York, and a conspiracy theory about a frozen envelope has outlived every attempt to check it — no evidence has ever surfaced.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: theScore, '30-year anniversary of conspiracy-laden 1985 NBA Draft Lottery'; Bleacher Report, 'The Frozen Envelope'

facts.headline: Wilt Chamberlain once took 55 rebounds off one basketball game.
facts.body: 24 November 1960, against Bill Russell's Celtics. It is still the record, and the man who set it said afterwards he had never been more tired in his life.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: HISTORY, 'Wilt Chamberlain sets NBA rebounds record'; Basketball-Reference box score, 24 November 1960

facts.headline: The single-game assist record belongs to a player most fans could not name.
facts.body: Scott Skiles handed out 30 for Orlando against Denver on 30 December 1990. It has stood for over thirty years.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: NBA.com, 'This Day in History: Scott Skiles Records 30 Assists in a Game'

facts.headline: Kobe Bryant scored 81 points in a regular-season game his team won by 18.
facts.body: 22 January 2006, the Lakers beating Toronto 122–104. It is the highest single-game total of the post-merger era outside Wilt Chamberlain's 100.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: Wikipedia, 'Kobe Bryant's 81-point game'; NBA.com 20th-anniversary retrospective

facts.headline: The tallest and the shortest men in NBA history are separated by two feet and four inches.
facts.body: Manute Bol and Gheorghe Mureșan both stood 7 feet 7. Muggsy Bogues was 5 feet 3, played fourteen seasons, and was never the worst defender on the floor.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: Guinness World Records, 'Tallest NBA player (ever)'; Britannica, 'List of the Tallest NBA Players'; NPR, 'The NBA's shortest player never gave up'; Basketball-Reference listing

facts.headline: Reggie Miller scored eight points in nine seconds, and the Knicks were leading by six when he started.
facts.body: Game 1 of the 1995 Eastern Conference semi-finals at Madison Square Garden: a three, a steal off the inbound, another three, then two free throws. Indiana won 107–105.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: NBA.com Pacers oral history, 'I Almost Fell Over'; Wikipedia, '8 points in 9 seconds'

facts.headline: Tracy McGrady scored thirteen points in the last thirty-five seconds and turned a loss into a win.
facts.body: 9 December 2004, Houston trailing San Antonio. Four straight three-pointers, one of them a four-point play, the last of them with two seconds left. Rockets 81–80.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: NBA.com, 'This Date In History: Tracy McGrady Scores 13 Points in 33 Seconds'; Wikipedia, '13 points in 35 seconds'

facts.headline: The Los Angeles Lakers are named after lakes a thousand miles away.
facts.body: The franchise began in Minneapolis and took its name from Minnesota, the Land of 10,000 Lakes. It moved to a city with almost none in 1960 and kept the name.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: Britannica, 'Los Angeles Lakers'; Star Tribune on the Minneapolis-to-Los Angeles move

facts.headline: Utah's team is called the Jazz because it used to be in New Orleans.
facts.body: The name was chosen there in 1974 for its dictionary meaning — collective improvisation — and travelled to Salt Lake City with the franchise in 1979. New Orleans has asked for it back.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: Britannica, 'Utah Jazz'; Deseret News and Deadspin accounts of the New Orleans naming and the move

facts.headline: Vancouver's NBA team was almost called the Mounties, until the Mounties objected.
facts.body: The Royal Canadian Mounted Police blocked the name, so the 1995 expansion side became the Grizzlies after the bear native to British Columbia. The franchise moved to Memphis in 2001 and kept it.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: Wikipedia, 'Vancouver Grizzlies' and 'History of the Memphis Grizzlies'

facts.headline: Toronto's team is named after a dinosaur from a film released the year before.
facts.body: Jurassic Park came out in 1993; the expansion franchise arrived in 1995 as the Raptors. The plaza outside their arena is still called Jurassic Park.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: EBSCO Research, 'Toronto Raptors'; CBC, 'The birth of the Toronto Raptors (as a logo)'

facts.headline: The NBA fined Michael Jordan for his shoes, and Nike decided that was the advertisement.
facts.body: The league's uniform rule required footwear to be mostly white and to match a player's teammates. Nike paid the fines, filmed a commercial about the ban, and the shoe became the best-known in the sport.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: Nike, 'How the Air Jordan 1 Banned Colorway Sparked a Sneaker Revolution'; Complex, 'The History of Michael Jordan's Banned Sneakers'. NOTE: published accounts disagree on the fine amount ($1,000 vs $5,000 per game), so no figure is stated in the copy.

facts.headline: The slam dunk contest was invented as a half-time filler by a league about to fold.
facts.body: 27 January 1976, at the ABA All-Star Game in Denver. Five players entered; Julius Erving won it. The ABA merged into the NBA that summer, and the contest, the three-point line and Erving all came with it.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: Wikipedia, 'Slam Dunk Contest'; ESPN Page 2, 'The day the dunk was born'

facts.headline: A 1993 arcade cabinet taught a generation of fans who NBA players were.
facts.body: NBA Jam put two players a side, no fouls, and a ball that caught fire. It was the highest-grossing arcade game of its year and the first mass-market NBA product that was not a broadcast.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: Wikipedia, 'NBA Jam (1993 video game)'; arcade-history.com entry

facts.headline: The first basketball shoe is still on sale, 108 years later.
facts.body: Converse launched the All Star in 1917. A journeyman player named Chuck Taylor sold it so well the company put his signature on it in 1932 — the shoe still carries the name of a man who was never a star.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: Nike/Converse, 'The True History of the Chuck Taylor All Star'; Naismith Hall of Fame biography of Chuck Taylor

facts.headline: One team won the first four championships the WNBA ever held.
facts.body: The Houston Comets took 1997, 1998, 1999 and 2000. The franchise folded in 2008; no WNBA team has won four in a row since.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: WNBA.com Sheryl Swoopes career timeline; Naismith Hall of Fame biography

facts.headline: Shai Gilgeous-Alexander is the first player in four years to win back-to-back MVPs.
facts.body: He took 83 of the 100 first-place votes for 2025-26 after averaging 31.1 points on a career-best 55.3% shooting for a 64-18 Oklahoma City team. He is the fourteenth player to repeat, and the first since Nikola Jokić in 2021 and 2022.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: NBA.com 2025-26 Kia MVP announcement; ESPN and NBC Sports reports on the full voting ballot

facts.headline: New York won a championship fifty-three years after its last one.
facts.body: The Knicks beat San Antonio 4-1 in the 2026 Finals, closing the series 94-90 in Game 5. Their previous title came in 1973, six years before the NBA had a three-point line.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: NBA.com 2026 NBA Finals coverage; ESPN report on Game 5

facts.headline: Jalen Brunson scored 45 points in the game that ended the Finals.
facts.body: All eleven voters gave him the 2026 Finals MVP after he averaged 32.6 points in the series. Only Michael Jordan, Bob Pettit and Giannis Antetokounmpo had scored 45 in a Finals closeout before him.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: NBA.com, 'Jalen Brunson wins Bill Russell trophy as 2026 NBA Finals MVP'; ESPN Game 5 report

facts.headline: No Defensive Player of the Year had ever been unanimous until 2026.
facts.body: Victor Wembanyama took all 100 first-place votes at 22, the youngest winner the award has had, after leading the NBA in blocks for a third straight season. He arrived from France in 2023 and is the third player, after Michael Jordan and David Robinson, to win both Rookie of the Year and this.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: NBA.com, 'Spurs' Victor Wembanyama named 2025-26 Kia NBA Defensive Player of the Year'; ESPN and CBS Sports voting reports

facts.headline: The youngest fifty-point game in NBA history belongs to a rookie.
facts.body: Cooper Flagg scored 51 against Orlando on 3 April 2026, aged 19 years and 103 days. Nobody younger had reached fifty in a league game.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: NBA.com 2025-26 Kia Rookie of the Year release; Associated Press report on Flagg's 51-point game

facts.headline: For the first time since Michael Jordan, a rookie led his own team in points, rebounds, assists and steals.
facts.body: Cooper Flagg averaged 21.0 points, 6.7 rebounds and 4.5 assists across 70 starts for Dallas and won Rookie of the Year for 2025-26. Jordan's 1984-85 season was the last time a first-year player topped his team in all four.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: NBA.com, 'Cooper Flagg named 2025-26 Kia NBA Rookie of the Year'; ESPN voting report

facts.headline: The 2026 scoring champion had been traded fourteen months earlier.
facts.body: Luka Dončić averaged 33.5 points a game for the Los Angeles Lakers in 2025-26. Dallas had sent him west in February 2025, in the middle of a season, in one of the largest deals the league has made.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: NBA.com 2025-26 season statistics; ESPN reporting on the February 2025 trade

facts.headline: San Antonio reached the Finals for the first time since 2014, with a 22-year-old as its best player.
facts.body: The Spurs won 62 games in 2025-26, the second-best record in the league, and lost the Finals 4-1 to New York.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: NBA.com 2026 playoff coverage; ESPN 2025-26 standings and season recap

facts.headline: Nobody had played twenty-three NBA seasons before.
facts.body: LeBron James passed Vince Carter's twenty-two in 2025-26, turned 41 during it, and finished the year with 43,440 regular-season points — a scoring record he has held since 2023.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: ESPN 2025-26 milestone tracker; Olympics.com LeBron James career points tracker

facts.headline: A record 135 international players opened an NBA season.
facts.body: The 2025-26 season began with 135 players from 43 countries on opening-night rosters, including a record 71 from Europe. France sent 19 of them and Australia 13.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: NBA.com, 'NBA rosters feature 135 international players from 43 countries to begin the 2025-26 season'

facts.headline: One player has four WNBA MVPs. Nobody else has more than three.
facts.body: A'ja Wilson won it in 2020, 2022, 2024 and 2025, passing Sheryl Swoopes, Lisa Leslie and Lauren Jackson. In 2025 she also led the league in scoring and won Defensive Player of the Year and Finals MVP — the first player in either league to take all four in one season.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: WNBA.com, 'A'ja Wilson Wins Record Fourth Kia WNBA Most Valuable Player Award'; ESPN and NPR coverage of the 2025 WNBA Finals

facts.headline: The Aces took a third title in four years without losing a Finals game.
facts.body: Las Vegas swept Phoenix in 2025, closing it out 97-86 on the road. A'ja Wilson scored 31 in the last one and made 17 of her 19 free throws.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: WNBA.com 2025 Finals coverage; NPR and Olympics.com reports on the deciding game

facts.headline: A rookie led the WNBA in assists.
facts.body: Caitlin Clark averaged 8.4 a game in 2024, more than anyone else in the league, along with 19.2 points and 5.7 rebounds. She won Rookie of the Year with 66 of the 67 votes.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: WNBA.com 2024 Rookie of the Year release; WNBA official 2024 season statistics

facts.headline: An expansion team made the playoffs in its first season.
facts.body: The Golden State Valkyries went 23-21 in 2025 and reached the postseason — the first WNBA expansion side to do either in its opening year.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: WNBA.com 2025 standings and playoff coverage; Associated Press reports on the Valkyries' inaugural season

facts.headline: Two WNBA players started their own league and it played its first season in a warehouse in Miami.
facts.body: Unrivaled, a three-on-three winter league founded by Napheesa Collier and Breanna Stewart, tipped off in January 2025. Rose BC beat Vinyl BC 62-54 in the first final.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: Unrivaled league announcements and Associated Press coverage of the inaugural 2025 season

facts.headline: Germany won a World Cup without losing a game, having never won anything before.
facts.body: The 2023 FIBA World Cup finished 8-0 for a German side that beat Serbia 83-77 in the final. Dennis Schröder was the tournament's most valuable player.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: FIBA.basketball 2023 World Cup final report; NBA.com coverage of Germany's title

facts.headline: One country won four European titles and two World Cups with more or less the same team.
facts.body: Spain took EuroBasket in 2009, 2011, 2015 and 2022 and the World Cup in 2006 and 2019, built around Pau and Marc Gasol and a group that had been winning together since junior tournaments in the late 1990s.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: FIBA.basketball tournament archives for EuroBasket and the FIBA World Cup

facts.headline: Slovenia won EuroBasket without losing a game, with an 18-year-old on the roster.
facts.body: The 2017 team went 9-0 for the country's first European title. Goran Dragić was named the tournament's most valuable player; the teenager beside him was Luka Dončić, who had not yet been drafted.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: FIBA.basketball EuroBasket 2017 tournament records and final report

facts.headline: A country that no longer exists won five basketball World Cups.
facts.body: Yugoslavia took the title in 1970, 1978 and 1990, and the federation that succeeded it won again in 1998 and 2002. The players from the 1990 squad went on to represent several different countries.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: FIBA.basketball World Cup archives

facts.headline: Only two players have won a EuroLeague title, an NBA championship and an Olympic gold medal.
facts.body: Manu Ginóbili won the EuroLeague with Virtus Bologna in 2001, the NBA title with San Antonio in 2003 and gold with Argentina in 2004. Bill Bradley had done it forty years earlier.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: EuroLeague Basketball and Naismith Hall of Fame biographies of Manu Ginóbili; FIBA records for the 2004 Olympic tournament

facts.headline: Canada's first World Cup medal came in overtime, against the United States.
facts.body: The 2023 bronze-medal game went to an extra period and Canada won it, Dillon Brooks scoring 39 and Shai Gilgeous-Alexander 31. It was the country's first medal at a senior global men's tournament since 1936.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: FIBA.basketball 2023 World Cup bronze-medal game report; Canada Basketball and NBA.com coverage

facts.headline: The first NBA game was played in Canada, and the league was not called the NBA.
facts.body: On 1 November 1946 the New York Knickerbockers beat the Toronto Huskies 68-66 at Maple Leaf Gardens, in front of 7,090 people. The competition was the Basketball Association of America; it took the NBA name three years later.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: NBA.com's account of the league's first game; The Canadian Encyclopedia entry on the Toronto Huskies

facts.headline: The NBA was created in an office in the Empire State Building.
facts.body: On 3 August 1949 the Basketball Association of America and the National Basketball League met in New York and agreed to merge. The league that resulted had seventeen teams, several of them in towns too small to keep one.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: History.com, 'NBA is born, August 3, 1949'; league records of the BAA-NBL merger

facts.headline: Three Black players entered the NBA in 1950, and which of them was first came down to the schedule.
facts.body: Earl Lloyd's Washington Capitols opened a day before Chuck Cooper's Celtics and Nat Clifton's Knicks, so Lloyd played the first game — 31 October 1950, six points, and a defeat. Cooper had been the first drafted; Clifton the first to sign a contract.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: NBA.com, 'Earl Lloyd, Chuck Cooper, Nat Clifton blaze new path in NBA'; Naismith Basketball Hall of Fame biography of Earl Lloyd

facts.headline: The first All-Star Game was staged to save the league's attention, and the host team's man won it.
facts.body: Celtics owner Walter Brown proposed the exhibition and offered Boston Garden for it. On 2 March 1951, 10,094 people watched the East win 111-94, and Boston's Ed Macauley was named most valuable player.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: NBA.com history of the 1951 All-Star Game; Guinness World Records entry for the first NBA All-Star Game

facts.headline: The first Black head coach in American professional sport also played centre for the team.
facts.body: Boston made Bill Russell player-coach in April 1966, succeeding Red Auerbach. He won championships in 1968 and 1969 while doing both jobs at once.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: History.com and Boston Celtics accounts of Bill Russell's appointment in April 1966

facts.headline: Bill Russell and Wilt Chamberlain played each other 142 times.
facts.body: Chamberlain outscored him in nearly all of them; Russell's teams won 85. Russell finished with eleven championships and Chamberlain with two.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: Basketball-Reference head-to-head records for Bill Russell and Wilt Chamberlain

facts.headline: Four teams survived the ABA, and one that did not made its owners a fortune anyway.
facts.body: The merger of June 1976 took in Denver, Indiana, New York and San Antonio. The Spirits of St. Louis folded, and their owners took a share of the four survivors' television money instead — a deal that kept paying for nearly forty years.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: History.com, 'NBA merges with ABA, June 17, 1976'; Washington Post reporting on the merger and the Spirits of St. Louis settlement

facts.headline: For sixteen years an NBA team could simply claim a college player who lived nearby.
facts.body: The territorial pick let a club give up its first-round choice and take anyone from within fifty miles of its arena. It is how Cincinnati got Oscar Robertson and Boston got Tom Heinsohn. The rule was abolished in 1966.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: Basketball-Reference NBA draft records, 1949-1965; NBA draft history on the territorial selection rule

facts.headline: A player had to win in the Supreme Court before anyone could enter the NBA early.
facts.body: Spencer Haywood signed with Seattle in 1970 while the league still required four years out of high school. The Supreme Court ruled in his favour in March 1971, and the hardship exception that followed is why later players could be drafted at nineteen.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: Haywood v. National Basketball Association, 401 U.S. 1204 (1971); NBA and Naismith Hall of Fame accounts of the hardship rule

facts.headline: The NBA has never officially said who is in its logo.
facts.body: Alan Siegel drew it in 1969 from a photograph of Jerry West and said so publicly in 2010. The league has never confirmed it, and West said he wished they would take him off it.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: NBA.com Q&A with Alan Siegel; Los Angeles Times 2010 interview and CBS Sports reporting on the logo's origin

facts.headline: The most-watched basketball game ever played was a college final.
facts.body: Michigan State beat Indiana State 75-64 on 26 March 1979 in front of a 24.1 television rating, still the highest for any basketball game at any level. It was the first time Magic Johnson and Larry Bird played each other.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source

facts.headline: The most famous floor in basketball was made out of scrap wood.
facts.body: Timber was short after the war, so in 1946 Boston built its court from offcuts of red oak: 247 panels bolted together, with dead spots visiting teams never got used to. It lasted until 1999.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: NBC Sports Boston and Wood Floor Business accounts of the Boston Garden parquet floor

facts.headline: Only one MVP has ever been unanimous.
facts.body: Stephen Curry took all 131 first-place votes in 2016, in a season where he made 402 three-pointers — 116 more than the record he had set himself the year before.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
